rationale: This fixes the crash from round 1 (I was writing into a read-only `.values` view) and keeps the same hypothesis. I z-score each genus's log relative abundance within each study, using the study label only for harmonization. The goal is to remove depth, 16S-region and protocol shifts, so the pooled random forest learns disease shifts rather than batch. The pseudocount is half a read at each sample's own depth.

Lower microbial diversity is one of the most consistent findings in IBD, but a random forest on genus abundances only sees it indirectly. I'm adding explicit alpha-diversity features alongside the unchanged genus relative abundances: Shannon and Simpson indices, plus richness after rarefying each sample to a fixed depth so sequencing depth doesn't drive the count. Scoring is within each study, so differences in diversity level between studies matter less than the case-vs-control drop inside each one.

I'm adding the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index as explicit features. It is the log-ratio of IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Veillonellaceae, Gemellaceae) to depleted taxa (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae), and I'm adding the log of each side too. A ratio within each sample cancels most per-study scaling, which per-study z-scoring (round 2) did not manage. It also condenses a known shift across many taxa into one feature, which the RF only finds piece by piece from single genus splits.

Right now every OTU with an empty genus (`g__`) is pooled into one column, so unclassified Lachnospiraceae, Enterobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae and others are mixed together, even though they move in opposite directions in IBD. This change gives each genus a key built from its full lineage, so unclassified reads stay with their family, and adds family-level and order-level relative abundances. The forest can then use the well-replicated family-level IBD shifts (Enterobacteriaceae up, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae down), which are also more consistent across studies with different 16S regions and classification depth.

Pooling four studies with different 16S regions creates hundreds of sparse genus, family and order columns that appear in only a few samples or a single study. With sqrt feature sampling these noisy, study-specific columns crowd out the informative taxa and the engineered dysbiosis and diversity features at each split. I'm adding a prevalence filter fitted on the training fold only: a taxon is kept if it is present in at least 10% of training samples. Diversity and dysbiosis-index features are always kept.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between the four studies, so the pooled forest gets rewarded for spotting which study a sample comes from (study-specific taxa, depth and region artefacts) instead of disease taxa. Within-study scoring can't benefit from that. I'm reweighting the training samples so each study × class cell carries equal total weight. Once that's done, the study label no longer predicts disease in the training data, and splits should go to signals that separate cases from controls within each study. The study label is used only for reweighting and never as a feature.

I'm adding an L2-regularized logistic regression on per-sample CLR genus abundances, with diversity and dysbiosis features standardized alongside them, and averaging its test-set ranks with the existing random forest. IBD dysbiosis is a broad shift across many taxa at once (butyrate producers down, Proteobacteria up). A linear model on log-ratios sees that whole shift together and ignores per-study scaling, while the forest only finds it piece by piece through threshold splits, so the two models' errors should only partly overlap.

The logistic regression currently sees only genus-level CLR, but the random forest gained +0.009 when family and order levels were added (round 5). Genus assignment depth differs across the four studies' 16S regions and pipelines, so I'm adding separately CLR-transformed family and order blocks (same training-fold prevalence filter) to the linear model. Under L2 this works like a hierarchical prior: genera from the same family share signal through the family term, which should make the broad IBD shifts (Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae down, Enterobacteriaceae up) more stable within each study.

For the logistic regression only, I centre each feature in its design matrix (CLR taxa, diversity, MDI) on the mean of that study's training-fold controls, and apply the same offset to that study's test samples. This follows the control-referenced normalization used to pool microbiome case–control studies (Gibbons 2018), and should remove study-level offsets from depth, 16S region and protocol while keeping each study's case-vs-control shift. Round 2 also used per-study z-scoring and lost score, but this differs: it centres on controls only and does not scale, so different case/control ratios across studies no longer shrink the disease signal. The random forest is unchanged.

I'm adding the control-centred CLR design (genus, family and order CLR plus diversity and dysbiosis-index features) to the random forest's inputs, next to its existing raw relative abundances. Centring each study on its own training-fold controls gave the logistic regression +0.006 in round 10, but the forest still splits on raw pooled abundances whose levels shift with each study's depth, 16S region and protocol. Unlike round 2, the centring uses controls only and doesn't rescale, so the forest can split on study-aligned "shift from that study's controls" values without losing the case signal in case-heavy studies.

The metric is AUROC computed within each study, but the RF and LR scores are currently rank-averaged over the whole pooled test fold. When one model squeezes a study's scores into a narrow band of pooled ranks (for example, the RF scoring all of one study's samples low because of that study's batch effects), the other model ends up deciding the ordering inside that study, so the 50/50 blend isn't really 50/50 there. This change ranks each model's scores within each test study before averaging, so both models get equal weight inside every study, and that within-study ordering is exactly what gets scored.

IBD involves losing whole taxa (fewer taxa are present), not just lower abundances. The CLR features blur this together with abundance and depth, because zeros get the same pseudocount at every depth. I'm adding genus presence/absence, measured after rarefying each sample to 1,000 reads so detection doesn't depend on sequencing depth, as an extra block for the logistic regression only. It is control-centred per study like the other features, and the random forest is unchanged. This is untested.

I'm adding a within-study dysbiosis score in the style of Lloyd-Price 2019 (iHMP), which is published but untested here: each sample's median Bray–Curtis and Aitchison distance from that study's training-fold controls. Training samples are scored leave-one-out, and the scores go into both the forest and the logistic regression. IBD microbiomes tend to be disturbed in different directions from patient to patient, so they sit far from the healthy cloud without sharing one shift. A distance to the study's own controls captures that, while the linear model and per-taxon forest splits can't, and it is unaffected by between-study depth and region offsets.

The four studies use different 16S regions and classifiers, so the same taxon can carry a different disease signal in each study, but the pooled logistic regression has to fit one shared coefficient per feature. I'm adding the multi-task setup from Daumé's "frustratingly easy" domain adaptation, which hasn't been tested here. Each standardized, control-centred feature gets a shared copy plus a copy that is non-zero only in its own study. Under L2, the per-study copies are pulled toward the shared effect, so each study can adjust its effect sizes. The study label still only changes how features are encoded. It never adds a per-study offset, so it can't act as a predictor, and the within-study metric would ignore one anyway.

I'm adding a regularized LightGBM booster on the same inputs as the random forest. The tree half of the blend becomes 0.25 RF + 0.25 GBM, and the logistic regression keeps its 0.5 weight, with every score still ranked within each test study. Boosting with shallow trees and strong shrinkage builds up small, consistent abundance and diversity shifts, while the bagged forest splits on single deep thresholds. Their errors should therefore only partly overlap, which should cut the variance of the tree side without diluting the linear model that has driven most of the recent gains.

Right now the rarefied genus presence/absence block (the one that helped the LR in round 13) and the rarefied richness features come from one random subsample to 1,000 reads, which throws away reads and adds sampling noise. That noise is worst for low-abundance taxa, and those are the ones whose loss marks IBD. I replace that single draw with its exact expected value under the hypergeometric distribution (Hurlbert-style rarefaction). For each genus this gives P(detected at 1,000 reads), and expected OTU and genus richness are sums of those probabilities. The features stay depth-normalized, become deterministic and less noisy, and the models are unchanged.

I'm replacing the fixed L2 strength of the logistic regression (C=0.05) with one picked by inner cross-validation on the training fold only. Grouping uses `groups_train` and folds are balanced by study×label. Each candidate C is scored with within-study AUROC, the same as the metric, and control-centring and scaling are refitted inside each inner fold. C=0.05 was chosen in round 8, when the design was a single genus CLR block. Since then I've added the family and order CLR blocks, the rarefied presence/absence block and per-study control-centring, which roughly triples the number of features and changes how strongly they're correlated, so the best amount of shrinkage has probably moved.

I'm extending the lineage-aware aggregation from genus/family/order up to class and phylum, adding them to both the random forest and the logistic regression (each as its own composition). Round 5's family/order aggregation gave the largest single gain. Some well-replicated IBD shifts (Gammaproteobacteria/Proteobacteria up, Firmicutes down) are at the class and phylum level, and those ranks are also classified most consistently across the four studies' different 16S regions and pipelines.

The logistic regression now scales each study's features by that study's training-fold control spread instead of only subtracting the control mean, so each feature becomes a z-score against that study's own controls (the control-referenced normalization of Gibbons 2018). Different 16S regions and depths change both the offset and the scale of the log-ratios (shallow studies have wider zero-driven CLR spread), and a single pooled coefficient can't fit both. The per-study SD is shrunk toward the pooled control SD so the small studies stay stable. This also differs from round 2, which z-scored over each study's cases and controls together, so its scaling shrank the signal in case-heavy studies.
